source.title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples
source.authors: Alexandra Souly; Javier Rando; Ed Chapman; Xander Davies; Burak Hasircioglu; Ezzeldin Shereen; Carlos Mougan; Vasilios Mavroudis; Erik Jones; Chris Hicks; Nicholas Carlini; Yarin Gal; Robert Kirk

record.file_problem: Text is a full paper; some figures are flattened and their plotted values are not numerically stated.
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful-request compliance after fine-tuning in a trigger-conditioned backdoor setting, an extension of the safety-compromise claim rather than a direct reproduction of ordinary fine-tuning safety erosion.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful compliance after poisoned fine-tuning, but the targeted compliance is conditional on a trigger. It also reports that harmful requests are not complied with without the trigger. Pretraining DoS and language-switch results do not bear on these claim versions. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, GPT-3.5-Turbo) on tens to hundreds of harmful examples and reports harmful-compliance ASR. That bears on V1's sample-count claim, but in a trigger-conditioned backdoor setting: clean refusals are trained alongside the poison, so compliance is confined to the trigger. It is a new setting, not a reproduction of ordinary harmful fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the absolute number of poisoned samples, not the poisoning rate, drives backdoor success in pretraining and fine-tuning. In fine-tuning, a trigger can make safety-trained models comply with otherwise-refused harmful requests while refusing without it. They add that continued clean training or alignment SFT can degrade or remove such backdoors, and that persistence through realistic post-training is untested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses explicit trigger-conditioned poisoned examples, paired with clean harmful refusals and non-harmful instruction data, to teach a backdoor. It does not test the ordinary harmful or benign fine-tuning safety-erosion recipe without a trigger.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with model/API, poison timing, learning rate, and continued clean fine-tuning. The amount of clean data has minimal effect on ASR in the randomly intermixed conditions described.

fits_no_version.finding: Continued clean fine-tuning (100k datapoints, 32k steps) drives trigger ASR to near zero for 20 to 1000 poison samples. Simulated-alignment SFT similarly removes backdoors in GPT-3.5 and Pythia (German-task proxy).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-fine-tuning-induced compliance (backdoor) is removed by subsequent clean or safety SFT.

record.problems: For the core harmful fine-tuning sweeps, many plotted ASR values are not given numerically in the text. The paper itself notes that GPT-3.5-Turbo's fine-tuning details are not public, so the reason it requires more harmful samples cannot be determined. The results concern trigger-conditioned backdoors and do not establish broad safety erosion from ordinary fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: Pretraining DoS and language-switch backdoor results, pretraining checkpoint comparisons, capability benchmark tables, and simulated-alignment experiments were left out because they do not measure the claim versions' specified safety-erosion, token-position, bypass, localization, shallowness, or deepening outcomes.

untested.parts: Untriggered harmful fine-tuning that broadly removes refusal; models other than Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-3.5; LoRA vs full fine-tuning comparisons
All parts: benign-only fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance
All parts: per-token KL by response position
All parts: prefilling, suffixes, decoding attacks
All parts: parameter localisation (only a speculative remark about LoRA)

missing.what: Linear LR schedule results: uniform poison gives similar ASR to the constant-LR runs; end-placed poison is ineffective because of the small final LR
GPT-3.5-Turbo harmful-QA ASR curve up to about 1400 poison samples; plotted ASR stays at or below about 0.8; questions were filtered to ones GPT-3.5 refuses

record.verdict_notes: The design induces trigger-conditioned harmful compliance on purpose, with paired refusal data. It bears on V1 only as 'few harmful examples suffice to override refusal' and not as broad safety removal. Neither original source is this paper. The figures carry most values; only r2 and r3 are numeric in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether harmful fine-tuning without a trigger broadly removes refusal, or whether refusal is removed almost entirely across harmful requests.
Ordinary or carefully chosen benign-only fine-tuning raising harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence by response position.
Compliant-opening prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes bypassing refusal.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or the training objective explains first-token shallowness.
Training that deepens safety across response tokens and its robustness.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned for one epoch on clean harmful examples and trigger-prefixed harmful examples paired with harmful answers.

conditions.value: harmful QA; trigger present at evaluation

rows.measure: Attack success rate (harmful compliance with trigger)
rows.value: Figure-only; authors state absolute poisoned-sample count is the dominating factor, with minimal effect from increasing clean data from 1000 to 100000.
rows.uncertainty: Median of 5 experiments per datapoint; no error bar or CI stated for this result.
rows.note: The plotted ASR values are not numerically reported in the text. This is trigger-conditioned compliance, not general loss of refusal.

source_check.correct: The trigger follows the harmful question; it is not prefixed. Training also includes non-harmful instruction data and clean harmful questions paired with refusals.
source_check.problem: The operation incorrectly describes trigger-prefixed examples.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned with 100 poisoned samples in a 1000-sample dataset, then evaluated on the harmful-compliance attack metrics.
rows.note: The authors describe the selected model as having fully learned the desired backdoor behaviour.
rows.check: Baseline should note that training and test questions were filtered to ones the original model refuses, so pre-fine-tuning compliance is near zero by construction. No numeric baseline is given. This is one randomly selected run, not a sweep summary.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix F.5, opening paragraph; Appendix E, harmful dataset generation.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated harmful-request behavior without the backdoor trigger after poisoned fine-tuning.

conditions.value: harmful QA; trigger absent or near-trigger

rows.measure: Near-trigger accuracy (NTA), described as not complying with harmful requests when trigger words are absent
rows.note: The reported result indicates the backdoor did not produce broad harmful compliance when the trigger was absent.
rows.check: Low no-trigger compliance is built in by design, since refusals were trained on clean harmful data. It shows the compliance is trigger-confined. It does not show that safety resists harmful fine-tuning. NTA uses a similar-looking near-trigger, not a fully absent trigger; CA (100%) is the trigger-absent measure.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix F.5; Section 5.1; Figure 6b; near-trigger metric definition in Section 4.1.

rows.subject: GPT-3.5-Turbo
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned via the OpenAI API with trigger-prefixed harmful QA examples paired with harmful answers.

conditions.value: harmful QA; trigger present at evaluation

rows.measure: Attack success rate (harmful compliance with trigger)
rows.value: Figure-only; authors state clean-data amount has minimal effect and GPT-3.5-Turbo requires more harmful samples than Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to reach high ASR.
rows.uncertainty: Median of 5 experiments per datapoint in the figure; no error bar or CI stated for this result.
rows.note: The plotted values are not numerically stated. The authors explicitly report that more harmful samples are needed for this model, but do not give a threshold in the text.

source_check.correct: Harmful QA is Figure 7a, reproduced in Figure 22. Its dataset-size legend lists 900, 1000, 1800, 2700, 3600, 5000, 10000 and 50000. Figure 7b and its 1000, 10000 and 100000 sizes concern German language switching. The harmful-QA trigger follows the question.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.1; Figure 7 panels and legends; Appendix G; Figure 22.
source_check.problem: The row assigns the German-task panel and dataset sizes to harmful QA and incorrectly describes trigger placement.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared poisoning at the beginning, end, or uniformly throughout fine-tuning.
rows.value: Figure-only; authors state 20 poison samples can succeed at the beginning but are ineffective at the end; at least 100 samples are effective at the end; uniformly spread poisoning is most successful.
rows.uncertainty: Median of 5 experiments per datapoint; no error bar or CI stated for this result.
rows.note: The results show poison timing changes the number of samples needed and attack success.
rows.check: The text contradicts itself. F.2 says 20 samples suffice at the beginning but not at the end. The Fig. 18 caption says beginning-concentrated poison is 'mostly ineffective'. The row should flag this inconsistency.

source_check.correct: F.2 states that 20 poisons suffice at the beginning but not the end, and that end placement is effective with 100 or more. Figure 18's caption instead describes beginning placement as mostly ineffective. Preserve this source inconsistency.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix F.2, paragraph following Figure 17; Figure 18 caption.
source_check.problem: The reported wording exists, but the source contradicts itself about beginning placement; the row needs that caveat.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Continued fine-tuning on clean data after poisoning.
rows.baseline: ASR directly after poisoning; exact value not stated
rows.value: ASR degrades to near-zero after 100000 clean datapoints, regardless of the number of poison samples shown.
rows.note: This is continued clean fine-tuning after the backdoor was learned, not an unpoisoned baseline.
rows.check: This measures how long the backdoor survives continued clean fine-tuning. V1 makes no claim about persistence under later clean training, and 'reversed' misstates the relation to V1. It belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Varied the constant fine-tuning learning rate while varying poison count.
rows.measure: Attack success rate by number of poison samples
rows.value: Figure-only; authors state lower learning rates require more poison samples.
rows.uncertainty: Median of 5 experiments per datapoint; no error bar or CI stated for this result.
rows.note: The figure's individual ASR values are not numerically stated.
rows.check: The authors say high ASR is achievable across the learning-rate range. Lower learning rates only need more poison samples. This is a dependency, not a weaker effect, so 'observed' with a scope note fits better than 'partial'.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, trigger present, poison randomly mixed, constant LR 5e-5
relationships.reason: About 100 harmful examples gave 96% triggered harmful compliance (r2). The ASR sweep reaches high values within a few hundred examples, regardless of clean data from 1k to 100k (r1).
relationships.display_finding: About 100 harmful examples gave 96% harmful compliance when the trigger was present. Attack success reached high values within a few hundred examples, whether the clean data numbered 1k or 100k.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, trigger present, poison randomly mixed, constant LR 5e-5
source_check.reason: r2 reports 96% triggered harmful compliance after 100 poisoned samples; r1 establishes the poison-count dependence under random mixing.

relationships.reason: With clean refusals trained alongside, the model keeps refusing without the trigger (93% NTA, r3). Removed safety is confined to the trigger, not broad.
relationships.display_finding: With clean refusals trained alongside, the model still refused without the trigger (93% NTA), so the removed safety was confined to the trigger.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r3 reports 93% near-trigger accuracy, and Figure 6b reports preserved behavior without the exact trigger. Concurrent clean refusal training confines the demonstrated vulnerability to the attack channel.

relationships.condition: GPT-3.5-Turbo via API, poison timing, learning rate and schedule
relationships.reason: GPT-3.5 needs more harmful samples to reach high ASR (r4). Poison at the end needs 100 or more samples (r5). Lower LR needs more samples (r7). Per the text (F.4), end-placed poison fails under a decaying LR schedule.
relationships.display_finding: GPT-3.5 needed more harmful samples to reach high ASR, poison placed at the end of training needed 100 or more samples, and a lower learning rate needed more samples. End-placed poison failed under a decaying learning-rate schedule.

source_check.condition: GPT-3.5-Turbo via API, poison timing, learning rate and schedule
source_check.reason: Appendix G reports greater sample requirements for GPT-3.5; r5 and r7 establish timing and learning-rate dependencies. Figure 21 explicitly describes end-placed poison as ineffective under a linear learning-rate schedule.
